intro: This page collects documented education, work and food programs in jails and prisons, the research on them, and the legal limits. Every figure has a source.

why.text: Suicide was the leading single cause of death in U.S. jails in 2019, at 49 deaths per 100,000 people held.
Release is the most dangerous moment: in Washington State, people's risk of death in their first two weeks out was 12.7 times that of other residents — and 129 times for drug overdose.
County budgets work out to about $75 a bed a day in Clark County, $78 in Garland County and $79 in Smith County, Texas (budget funds divided by rated beds: 49, 480 and 1,139).

items.name: Miami-Dade, Florida
items.text: Its court sends people in mental-health crisis to treatment instead of jail. Judge Steve Leifman says reoffending fell from 75% to 20% for misdemeanors and from 75% to 6% for felonies. These are the judge’s own figures as reported by WLRN; no independent evaluation was cited.

items.name: Bexar County, Texas
items.text: Its diversion center lets people choose treatment instead of jail — “a choice: jail or diversion.”

items.name: Portugal
items.text: Since 2001, possessing drugs for personal use has been handled by health-focused “dissuasion commissions” instead of criminal courts.

items.name: Rhode Island
items.text: After it began offering addiction medications throughout its correctional system, overdose deaths among recently released people fell 60.5%. The study’s authors estimated that treating about 11 people was associated with one fewer death.

ideas.group: Prison models built to resemble life outside

items.name: Germany
items.text: Its prison law says life inside should resemble ordinary life as far as possible.

items.name: Norway
items.text: Builds its prisons on a “principle of normality” — people keep their rights, and services come from the same community services everyone uses.

items.name: Bastøy, Norway
items.text: An island prison in southeast Norway; staff travel there by ferry and the men live in wooden cottages.

items.name: In the U.S.
items.text: Pennsylvania opened a “Little Scandinavia” unit at SCI Chester, and California renamed San Quentin the San Quentin Rehabilitation Center in 2023, putting rehabilitation and education first.

ideas.group: Programs run by the people held there

items.name: Brazil’s APAC prisons
items.text: The people held there guard themselves, cook, garden, and hold the keys to the front door, with a small staff. Their low reoffending figures are self-reported.

items.name: Amity, California
items.text: An in-prison therapeutic community: 43.3% returned to prison within two years, against 67.1% of a comparison group.

items.name: New Zealand
items.text: Restorative justice conferences bring the person who did harm together with the people harmed to agree on how to make it right.

items.name: Singapore
items.text: The Yellow Ribbon Project runs campaigns aimed at employers and the public as well as at people leaving prison. Its two-year reoffending rate for people released in 2023 was 21.9%, down from about 44% two decades earlier.

food.title: Jail and prison gardens and farms
food.lead: Some jails and prisons grow food on their own land. Examples, with the amounts each reports:

items.name: Smith County, Texas
items.text: Jail inmates run a garden on Highway 155 and give all of the produce to the East Texas Food Bank — in excess of 160,000 pounds, its CEO estimated. The sheriff: people are “sitting in line at the jail, wanting to get out here and work.”

items.name: Garland County, Arkansas
items.text: The detention center sits on 57 acres and is a University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture site, donating thousands of pounds of produce to Project Hope Food Bank.

items.name: Washington State Penitentiary
items.text: Its gardeners donated 243,822 pounds of produce to a local food bank.

items.name: Georgia
items.text: The source reports prison farms supply 43% of the food served to 60,000 people in 86 facilities, and all of the beef, pork, eggs and milk.

items.name: The Clink (UK)
items.text: Training restaurants inside prisons. A UK government evaluation found graduates committed fewer reoffenses — 23 per 100 people in a year, against 37 for a matched group — though about the same share reoffended at all.

evidence.text: People who took part in education while locked up had 43% lower odds of coming back — about 13 percentage points less risk.
Trade training did the most for jobs: employment after release was 28% higher than for people with no education inside.
Educating 100 people inside costs $140,000 to $174,400 and cuts their reincarceration costs by $870,000 to $970,000 — roughly $5 to $7 back for every $1.
Federal Pell Grants were restored for people in prison on July 1, 2023, through approved programs run by accredited colleges.

jails.text: Jails aren’t prisons: in 2023, 70% of people in U.S. jails had not been convicted, and the average stay was 32 days.

edges.text: The 13th Amendment still allows forced labor as punishment for a crime. Regular prison jobs in Arkansas and Texas are unpaid; nationally, incarcerated workers average 13 to 52 cents an hour.
Arkansas’s Cummins Unit was built in 1902 on land bought from the Cummins and Maple Grove plantations, and prison farm labor there has a documented history of forced labor.
Reveal’s 2017 investigation reported that courts in Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas and Missouri sent men to a “rehab” program where most worked full time at a poultry company.
Some licenses bar people with records; federal rules forbid Pell-funded programs from training for jobs that state law closes to them (34 CFR 668.236).
